questions.stem: What physiological change do astronauts on the Space Station experience?
options: Growth in leg muscle strength from constantly pushing off surfaces
Blood pooling in the feet and lower legs from stronger downward forces
Loss of bone density and muscle mass, needing daily exercise to limit it
Thickening of bones, since they no longer flex under body weight
questions.explanation: In continuous free fall, bones and muscles are no longer loaded by body weight, so the body reduces bone mineral and muscle tissue it appears not to need — which is why resistance and treadmill exercise is scheduled every day. The claim that bones thicken because they no longer flex reverses the actual cause: it is loading and flexing that stimulates bone to stay dense. In fact fluids shift upward toward the head in microgravity, not down into the legs.

questions.stem: Why are telescopes like Hubble and James Webb placed above Earth's atmosphere?
options: Without air resistance the mirrors can be made to magnify far more strongly
Starlight only travels in straight lines outside a planet's gravity
The atmosphere absorbs and distorts incoming light, blurring the images
Being above the atmosphere puts them much closer to distant galaxies
questions.explanation: Air turbulence smears images and atmospheric gases absorb large parts of the infrared and ultraviolet spectrum, so an orbiting telescope receives sharper, more complete light. The 'closer to distant galaxies' option sounds sensible but a few hundred kilometres is negligible against distances of millions of light years. The test to apply is whether the atmosphere is doing something to the light, not whether the telescope has moved a useful distance.

questions.stem: When Mars is about 225 million kilometres from Earth, roughly how long does a radio signal take to travel one way? (Radio waves travel at about 300 000 km/s.):
options: Essentially no time, since radio is instantaneous
About 12.5 minutes
About 12.5 seconds
About 2 hours
questions.explanation: Time equals distance divided by speed: 225 000 000 ÷ 300 000 = 750 seconds, which is 12.5 minutes, so a question and its answer take about 25 minutes to return. The '12.5 seconds' option comes from dropping a factor of 60 when converting, and it is worth checking whether the answer in seconds is larger than 60. This delay is exactly why Mars rovers and crews must be able to make decisions without waiting for mission control.

questions.stem: Light from almost all distant galaxies is shifted towards the red end of the spectrum, and the shift is greater for more distant galaxies. What does this indicate?
options: Distant galaxies are moving towards us and crowding into the centre of the universe
Space is expanding, so more distant galaxies are receding from us more rapidly
Distant galaxies are all rotating faster than nearby galaxies are
Distant galaxies are made mainly of red stars while nearby ones are made of blue stars
questions.explanation: Wavelengths of light from a receding source are stretched, and the systematic increase of redshift with distance shows recession speed rises with distance — the signature of expanding space. The 'made of red stars' option confuses the colour of an object with a shift in the position of its spectral lines; redshift is measured by identifying known lines and seeing how far they have moved. Motion towards an observer would produce a blueshift, the opposite of what is observed.

questions.stem: In 2019 an international team released the first image of a black hole, at the centre of the galaxy M87. What did the image actually show?
options: Light emitted from the black hole's singularity, made visible by combining many telescopes
A dense spherical star so massive that its surface glows white across all wavelengths
The gravitational waves produced as the black hole swallowed a neighbouring star
A bright ring of hot glowing gas surrounding a dark region the size of the event horizon
questions.explanation: Nothing escapes from inside the event horizon, so the image is of superheated material orbiting outside it, with a dark 'shadow' where light is captured or bent away. The option about light from the singularity is the common trap: it assumes a black hole can be seen directly, when in fact black holes are detected only by their effect on nearby matter and light. Gravitational waves are a separate kind of detection, measured by instruments like LIGO rather than photographed.

questions.stem: Designs for long-duration spacecraft often include a large rotating ring section. What is the scientific reasoning behind this?
options: Spinning generates a magnetic field around the ring which pulls the crew towards the floor
Rotating increases the spacecraft's total mass, so its own gravitational pull becomes noticeable
Spinning cancels the microgravity of orbit so that Earth's real gravity can reach the crew
Rotation forces the walls to push crew inwards along a circular path, and this push feels like weight
questions.explanation: An object moving in a circle needs a force directed towards the centre; in a rotating habitat the outer wall supplies that force, so crew standing on it feel pressed against a 'floor' much as they do under gravity. The idea that rotation lets Earth's real gravity reach the crew is tempting but wrong, because astronauts in orbit are already within Earth's gravity — they float because they are in continuous free fall. Rotation also cannot change a spacecraft's mass or create a gravitational field of useful strength.

questions.stem: Why do missions to Jupiter and Saturn use robotic probes rather than astronauts?
options: Probes transmit data instantly, while a crewed craft's signals are delayed
Crewed spacecraft cannot escape Earth's gravity, so only probes leave
The outer planets have no solid surface, so a crew could not refuel
The journeys take years, so carrying food, air and shielding is impractical
questions.explanation: Crewed missions must carry consumables and shielding for the whole trip, and journeys to the outer planets take many years, so mass, cost and crew safety currently rule them out; robots need no air, food or return journey. The claim that probes transmit data instantly is wrong — all radio signals travel at the speed of light, so data from Saturn takes over an hour either way. Cue: any option saying a signal arrives 'instantly' across the solar system is false, because the speed of light is finite.

questions.stem: What is the cosmic microwave background?
options: Faint microwave radiation from every direction, released as the early universe cooled
Microwave radiation streaming outwards from the supermassive black hole in our galaxy
The combined microwave glow of all the stars in all observable galaxies
Microwave emissions from dust clouds in the plane of our own galaxy
questions.explanation: The cosmic microwave background is leftover radiation from a hot, dense early universe, released when it cooled enough for atoms to form, and it reaches us almost uniformly from all directions. The 'combined glow of all the stars' option is tempting because starlight does fill the sky, but the background is far too smooth and too cold to come from individual sources, and it exists between galaxies as well. Cue: uniform in every direction and traced to the whole early universe, not to any object within it.

questions.stem: Why is radiation a bigger hazard on a Mars trip than on the Space Station?
options: Radiation only affects a craft once past Earth's escape speed
The craft spends months outside Earth's magnetic field, which deflects particles
There is no air in interplanetary space, and air absorbs radiation
The Sun's radiation grows more intense with distance as Mars nears
questions.explanation: Earth's magnetic field deflects a large fraction of charged particles from the Sun and from deep space, and the space station orbits largely within its protection; a Mars-bound craft leaves that shelter for months. The 'no air in space' option is wrong because the space station also orbits in effectively a vacuum — it is the magnetic field, not air, that makes the difference. Cue: link protection to Earth's magnetic field and the duration of exposure.

questions.stem: On the International Space Station, water vapour from the crew's breath and sweat, and urine, are processed and returned to the drinking water supply. Why is such recycling essential for long-duration missions?
options: Recycled water is chemically different from Earth water and is better absorbed by the body in microgravity
Resupply from Earth is slow and costly, so a nearly closed loop reduces the mass of water that must be launched
Water taken from Earth breaks down into hydrogen and oxygen in microgravity and must be reassembled
Drinking water stored for more than a few weeks freezes solid in orbit and cannot be thawed on board
questions.explanation: Every kilogram lifted to orbit costs fuel and money, so closing the loop on water, and eventually food and air, is the only practical way to sustain crews far from Earth. The idea that water 'breaks down in microgravity' is wrong — microgravity affects how liquids behave and where they collect, not the chemical stability of the molecule. Cue: life-support design is driven by launch mass, not by chemistry changing in space.

questions.stem: Astronomers can state which elements are present in a distant star without ever collecting a sample from it. Which technique makes this possible?
options: Measuring the total brightness of the star and comparing it with the brightness of the Sun
Timing how long the star's light takes to reach Earth and calculating its density from the delay
Recording the star's exact colour and matching it to the colour each element glows when burned
Splitting the star's light into a spectrum and identifying the pattern of dark absorption lines
questions.explanation: Each element absorbs light at a characteristic set of wavelengths, so dark lines at particular positions in a star's spectrum act as a fingerprint of the gases in its outer layers. Matching overall colour to a flame colour is tempting because flame tests are familiar, but a star's overall colour indicates its surface temperature, and the light of many elements blended together gives no single element's colour. Cue: composition comes from the pattern of lines, temperature from the overall colour.

questions.stem: Missions to Mars can only be launched during a window that occurs roughly every 26 months. What causes these windows?
options: The gravitational pull between Earth and Mars reverses direction on a 26-month cycle, blocking travel in between
Earth and Mars orbit the Sun at different rates, so the alignment giving the shortest, lowest-fuel path recurs periodically
Mars only comes within range of Earth's rockets every 26 months; at other times it is beyond their maximum reach
Earth's rotation carries launch sites into the correct direction to face Mars only about once every two years
questions.explanation: Mars takes about 687 days to orbit the Sun and Earth about 365, so the favourable relative positions for a low-energy transfer repeat about every 26 months. The 'beyond maximum reach' option is wrong because a rocket's capability is not a fixed distance limit — a craft could be sent at other times, but the journey would need far more fuel for the same payload. Cue: launch windows are about efficient trajectories set by orbital positions, not about rockets running out of range.

questions.stem: The James Webb Space Telescope has imaged galaxies whose light has travelled for more than 13 billion years. Why does observing such distant galaxies help scientists study the early universe?
options: Galaxies further away are physically younger objects that formed only recently, unlike the older nearby ones
The extreme distance stretches the light so much that it carries a direct record of every stage of the galaxy's life
Distant galaxies move too slowly to have changed at all, so their present appearance still matches the early universe
Light takes time to travel, so the image shows those galaxies as they were billions of years ago, not as they are now
questions.explanation: Because light has a finite speed, looking further out means looking further back in time — an object 13 billion light-years away is seen as it was 13 billion years ago. The claim that distant galaxies are 'younger objects that formed recently' reverses the idea: they are seen at an early stage of their lives, but they formed long ago and may look very different now. Cue: distance in space equals lookback time, so telescopes act as time machines.

questions.stem: What is the main scientific purpose of rover missions like Perseverance on Mars?
options: To release oxygen into the atmosphere so humans can breathe there
To test whether Mars can be pushed into a warmer orbit
To confirm Mars has no moons and therefore no tidal effects
To analyse rocks and soil for signs Mars once supported microbial life
questions.explanation: Robotic rovers carry laboratories that examine Martian rock chemistry, minerals and sediments for evidence of past liquid water and conditions suitable for life, expanding knowledge that cannot be gained from orbit. Releasing oxygen to make the atmosphere breathable is not a rover's purpose; small experiments have made tiny amounts of oxygen for testing technology, not for terraforming. Mars also has two moons, Phobos and Deimos, so that option is factually wrong. The cue is that current Mars missions gather data and test technology, they do not modify the planet.

questions.stem: Astronomers describe distances to stars and galaxies in light-years. A light-year is:
options: the distance the Earth travels along its orbit in one year
the time taken for one full rotation of our galaxy
the distance light travels through space in one year
the time light takes to reach Earth from the nearest star
questions.explanation: A light-year is a unit of distance, equal to how far light travels in a year at about 300 000 km per second, roughly 9.5 trillion kilometres. The tempting error is reading the word 'year' as a measure of time, as in 'the time light takes to reach Earth from the nearest star' — that is about 4.2 years, a duration, not a distance. The cue is that any unit built from a speed multiplied by a time is a distance.

questions.stem: Why do Space Station crew do about two hours of exercise daily?
options: To use up excess oxygen so the cabin air mixture stays balanced
To strengthen the heart against the crushing forces of orbital speed
To slow the loss of bone density and muscle mass in microgravity
To keep their body temperature up, since space outside is very cold
questions.explanation: Without the constant loading that gravity provides, weight-bearing bones and muscles weaken measurably within weeks, so daily loaded exercise is a countermeasure that limits the loss. Warming the body is not the issue: the station is temperature controlled and the crew's problem is usually removing excess heat, not generating it. Orbital speed itself is not felt as a force, because the station and crew are in continuous free fall together.

questions.stem: Probes such as Voyager and Cassini were sent past planets on carefully chosen paths so that each close approach increased the probe's speed. What makes this 'gravity assist' work?
options: Sunlight reflected from the planet's cloud tops pushes the probe forwards
The probe gains speed from the planet's motion around the Sun as it swings past
The probe collects hydrogen from the planet's upper atmosphere and burns it
The planet's magnetic field repels the probe's metal hull and accelerates it
questions.explanation: In a gravity assist the spacecraft is pulled in and flung out by the planet's gravity, and because the planet is itself moving around the Sun the probe leaves with extra speed relative to the Sun, with the planet losing an utterly negligible amount. Magnetic repulsion of a spacecraft hull is not a real effect at these scales and would not provide useful thrust. The cue is that the energy comes from the planet's orbital motion, not from fuel, fields or light.

questions.stem: Designs for a long-duration Mars base include greenhouses growing crops under artificial light. Besides food, what other life-support benefit does this provide?
options: Growing roots generate a weak downward pull that mimics Earth's gravity
Plant leaves block cosmic radiation from reaching the crew quarters
Transpiring plants remove nitrogen from the air, which is toxic to humans
Photosynthesis takes in carbon dioxide and releases oxygen into the cabin air
questions.explanation: Plants photosynthesise, consuming the carbon dioxide the crew exhales and releasing oxygen, so a greenhouse contributes to closing the air loop as well as the food loop. The idea that leaves shield cosmic radiation is wrong: effective shielding needs substantial mass such as water, regolith or hull material, not thin foliage. Nitrogen is also harmless in air and makes up most of what we breathe, so removing it is not a goal.

questions.stem: Astronomers measure how fast stars orbit in the outer parts of spiral galaxies and find they move much faster than the visible matter can explain. What conclusion have astronomers drawn from this pattern?
options: Galaxies contain large amounts of unseen 'dark matter' adding extra gravity
The outer stars are being flung away and those galaxies are breaking apart
The light from outer stars is redshifted, making them appear to move fast
Those galaxies must be much closer to Earth than their brightness suggests
questions.explanation: If only the visible stars and gas supplied the gravity, orbital speeds should fall off with distance from the galactic centre, but they stay high, which implies a large halo of matter that emits no light. Saying the galaxies are flying apart is wrong: these are stable, long-lived structures whose stars remain gravitationally bound. Redshift measures motion along the line of sight and is the tool used to obtain the speeds, not an artefact that fakes them.

questions.stem: Mission planners for a crewed Mars landing propose making rocket propellant and oxygen on Mars from its atmosphere and ice, rather than carrying it all from Earth. Why is this approach so attractive?
options: Martian air is dense enough that a returning rocket needs almost no fuel
Every kilogram of return fuel carried from Earth adds far more launch mass at liftoff
Fuel manufactured on Mars burns hotter because Martian gravity is weaker
Rocket fuel spoils chemically within weeks, so it cannot survive the transit
questions.explanation: Propellant needed for the return trip must itself be lifted from Earth and carried the whole way, so it multiplies the mass, size and cost of the launch vehicle; producing it on site removes that penalty. The claim that fuel burns hotter in weaker gravity is false, since combustion temperature depends on the chemistry of the reactants, not on local gravity. Mars' atmosphere is also extremely thin, about one per cent of Earth's pressure, so it offers little help to a launching rocket.

questions.stem: A star such as the Sun shines because:
options: Hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium in its core, releasing energy
Hydrogen and oxygen burn in a chemical combustion reaction
Heavy elements in its core split apart in nuclear fission
Gas particles rubbing together create friction heat throughout it
questions.explanation: The enormous pressure and temperature in a star's core force hydrogen nuclei to fuse into helium, and the small loss of mass in each reaction is released as energy. 'Burning' in a chemical sense is the most common misconception — chemical reactions release far too little energy to keep a star shining for billions of years, and there is no oxygen supply in the core anyway. Fission splits heavy nuclei and powers reactors on Earth, not main-sequence stars.

questions.stem: Which list places these features in order from smallest to largest?
options: Star, solar system, galaxy, universe
Solar system, star, galaxy, universe
Star, galaxy, solar system, universe
Solar system, galaxy, star, universe
questions.explanation: A star is a single object; a solar system is one star plus everything orbiting it; a galaxy contains billions of such systems; and the observable universe contains hundreds of billions of galaxies. Placing the solar system before the star is the most common slip — a solar system must be larger than the star at its centre, because the star is only one part of it. Check each step by asking 'is this thing contained inside the next one?'

questions.stem: A star with about 25 times the mass of the Sun runs out of nuclear fuel in its core. What is the most likely outcome?
options: The star gently sheds its outer layers and settles down as a white dwarf
The star immediately becomes a black hole with no explosion or ejected material
The star cools and shrinks steadily until it becomes a large cold planet
The core collapses and the star explodes as a supernova, leaving a black hole
questions.explanation: Once fusion can no longer support a very massive star, its core collapses under gravity and the outer layers are blown off in a supernova; if the remaining core is massive enough, nothing can halt the collapse and a black hole forms. The white dwarf ending is tempting because it is a real stellar fate, but it applies to low- and medium-mass stars like the Sun, not to stars tens of times more massive. Use the star's mass as the cue for which path it takes.

questions.stem: A student says, 'The big bang was a huge explosion of matter into the empty space that was already there.' Why is this description scientifically inaccurate?
options: The big bang describes an explosion at one identifiable point, and astronomers have located that point in the Milky Way
The big bang describes the universe collapsing inwards from a large cold state to the hot dense state we now observe
The big bang describes space itself expanding from an extremely hot, dense state, not matter flying into pre-existing space
The big bang describes a slow, steady creation of matter that is still adding new galaxies to empty space today
questions.explanation: In big bang cosmology, space, time, matter and energy all originated together in an extremely hot, dense state, and it is space itself that has been expanding ever since — there was no surrounding empty space for material to explode into. The 'explosion at one identifiable point' option is the seductive one because it matches everyday explosions, but the expansion happens everywhere at once and no centre can be located. The cue is the word 'into': the big bang was not an explosion into anything.

questions.stem: From Earth, almost every distant galaxy appears to be moving away from us, and the further away it is the faster it recedes. What does this pattern tell us about our position?
options: Nothing special — observers in any galaxy would see the same pattern, because space is expanding everywhere
We are close to the centre of the universe, which is why other galaxies move away from us in all directions
We are at the edge of the universe, so galaxies can only ever recede from us and never approach
We are stationary while all other galaxies travel outwards through space away from a common origin point
questions.explanation: Because space itself stretches between galaxies rather than galaxies flying through space from a centre, every observer anywhere sees all distant galaxies receding, with speed increasing with distance. The 'we are near the centre' option is the classic trap — the observation looks centred on us, but that appearance is exactly what a uniformly expanding space produces for every observer. Think of dots on an inflating balloon: from any dot, all the others move away.

questions.stem: Which description best defines a galaxy?
options: A vast system of billions of stars, plus gas and dust, held together by gravity
A star with a family of planets, moons and asteroids orbiting around it
A cloud of gas and dust in space where new stars are formed
A group of bright stars that appear to form a pattern in Earth's night sky
questions.explanation: A galaxy is a gravitationally bound system containing huge numbers of stars along with interstellar gas and dust; our Milky Way is one of billions. The option describing a star with orbiting planets defines a solar system, which is far smaller and sits inside a galaxy. The star-forming cloud is a nebula, and a sky pattern of bright stars is a constellation, which is a line-of-sight effect rather than a physical system. Cue: if the description does not include billions of stars bound by gravity, it is not a galaxy.

questions.stem: Which everyday model best represents the expansion of the universe described by the big bang theory?
options: Marbles fired outwards from one point on a table, spreading out across the surface
Water spreading outwards across a floor from a spilled bucket at one spot
Smoke from a candle drifting upwards and outwards through the still air of a room
Dots drawn on a balloon's surface, which all move apart as the balloon is inflated
questions.explanation: In the big bang model space itself expands, so every observer sees other galaxies receding and there is no special centre — exactly what the dots on an inflating balloon show. The marbles fired from a point are the most tempting model, but they move through pre-existing space away from a definite centre, which is not how cosmic expansion works. The spilled water and drifting smoke share the same flaw: an identifiable starting point in space that everything moves away from.

questions.stem: In 2015 detectors recorded a brief gravitational wave signal matching the predicted merger of two black holes about 1.3 billion light-years away. What did this detection provide?
options: The first proof that the universe is expanding, since the wave had travelled 1.3 billion light-years
Evidence that black holes emit light when they merge, allowing them to be seen with optical telescopes
Confirmation that the cosmic microwave background is produced by black holes merging
Direct evidence that black holes exist as merging objects and that they produce ripples in spacetime
questions.explanation: Gravitational waves are disturbances in spacetime predicted to be produced when very massive compact objects orbit and merge, and the recorded signal matched the predicted pattern for two merging black holes, giving direct observational support for both the waves and the objects. Saying it proved cosmic expansion is wrong: expansion evidence comes from galaxy redshifts, and a long travel time alone shows nothing about expansion. Black hole mergers were detected through spacetime ripples, not light, and the cosmic microwave background is leftover radiation from the hot early universe.

questions.stem: Where does the Sun sit in the structure of the universe?
options: The Milky Way is the whole universe, and other 'galaxies' are clusters in it
One of hundreds of billions of stars in the Milky Way, itself one of billions
At the centre of the Milky Way, with the galaxy's stars orbiting around it
At the centre of the universe, with all galaxies moving outwards from it
questions.explanation: Our solar system is one planetary system around one fairly ordinary star, located out in a spiral arm of the Milky Way, and the Milky Way itself is only one of an enormous number of galaxies. The option placing the Sun at the galaxy's centre is tempting because planets do orbit the Sun, but the Sun in turn orbits the galactic centre, which is tens of thousands of light-years away. Keep the nesting order in mind: planets orbit a star, stars orbit within a galaxy, galaxies spread through the universe.

questions.stem: A star with about the same mass as the Sun uses up the hydrogen in its core. What is the most likely sequence of events?
options: It swells into a red giant, sheds its outer layers as a glowing shell of gas, and leaves a hot white dwarf
It swells into a red giant, explodes as a supernova, and leaves a rapidly spinning neutron star behind
It contracts smoothly and steadily until its own gravity crushes it into a stellar-mass black hole
It cools and fades in place over a few thousand years without changing size, ending as a dark rocky body
questions.explanation: Sun-like stars are not massive enough for the runaway core collapse that drives a supernova; instead the core contracts and heats while the outer layers expand into a red giant, are then puffed away, and the exposed core remains as a white dwarf. The supernova-and-neutron-star option is the classic mix-up, but that fate needs a star many times the Sun's mass. The cue is mass: low-to-medium mass gives red giant then white dwarf, high mass gives supernova then neutron star or black hole.

questions.stem: Most of the carbon in your body and the iron in Earth's core were not made in the big bang. Where did these elements come from?
options: They condensed directly out of the cosmic microwave background as the early universe cooled
They were produced in the first three minutes after the big bang, along with hydrogen and helium
They formed inside Earth over billions of years as lighter elements were compressed by gravity
They were built up by nuclear fusion inside stars and spread through space when those stars died
questions.explanation: The early universe was only hot and dense long enough to make the lightest elements, so heavier elements such as carbon, oxygen and iron were fused later in the cores of stars and scattered by stellar winds and supernova explosions. The option that they formed in the first three minutes is the tempting one, but by then the universe had expanded and cooled too much for fusion to continue past helium and traces of lithium. The cue is: light elements from the big bang, heavier elements from generations of stars.

questions.stem: Astronomers can detect black holes even though no light escapes from them. Which approach is actually used?
options: Watching for the moment a black hole passes in front of the Milky Way and blocks out a whole star field
Bouncing powerful radar pulses off the black hole and timing how long the echo takes to return
Observing stars whipping around an unseen massive object and X-rays from gas heated as it spirals inwards
Detecting the faint light emitted directly from the surface of the black hole using infrared telescopes
questions.explanation: Because the black hole itself emits nothing, astronomers infer it from its effects: the fast orbits of nearby stars reveal a large mass in a tiny volume, and gas falling in forms a hot disc that radiates X-rays. Detecting light from its surface is impossible by definition, since anything inside the event horizon cannot send radiation out. The cue is to look for evidence of gravitational influence and heated surrounding matter, not for direct emission from the object.

questions.stem: The cosmic microwave background was released when the universe was extremely hot, yet today it is detected as faint microwaves at about 3 degrees above absolute zero. What best explains this?
options: The radiation has lost energy by colliding with dust and gas clouds spread throughout intergalactic space
The radiation was always microwave radiation, because the early universe was cold before stars formed
Distant galaxies absorb the visible light from it and re-emit the energy at microwave wavelengths
The expansion of space has stretched the radiation's wavelengths as the universe cooled over billions of years
questions.explanation: Radiation released when the young universe became transparent was far more energetic, but as space itself expanded the wavelengths were stretched, so it now arrives as low-energy microwaves corresponding to a very low temperature. The suggestion that it lost energy by colliding with dust is tempting because scattering does affect light, but the background is remarkably uniform across the whole sky, which is what expansion of space predicts rather than patchy absorption. The cue is that stretching wavelengths is the same mechanism as redshift, applied to the whole universe.

questions.stem: Which observation, if it were reliably confirmed, would most seriously challenge the big bang theory?
options: A galaxy whose light has taken about 12 billion years to reach telescopes on and above Earth
A black hole found to be far more massive than models of galaxy centres had predicted
A rocky planet discovered orbiting a star in a distant part of the Milky Way's outer disc
A star in our own galaxy shown by several independent methods to be about 20 billion years old
questions.explanation: Evidence indicates the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago, so a confirmed object older than that could not fit within the model and would force a major rethink. The very distant galaxy option looks impressive but sits comfortably inside 13.8 billion years, so it is exactly what the theory expects. The cue for a genuine challenge is a result that contradicts a specific prediction of the model, such as its age, its expansion, or the proportions of light elements.

questions.stem: What is a solar system?
options: A star with the planets, moons and other objects orbiting it
A cluster of billions of stars, gas and dust bound by gravity
A cold cloud of gas and dust in which new stars are forming
A group of galaxies held together by mutual gravitational attraction
questions.explanation: A solar system is a single star and everything gravitationally bound in orbit around it — planets, moons, dwarf planets, asteroids and comets. The option describing billions of stars with gas and dust is the definition of a galaxy, which is vastly larger and contains hundreds of billions of solar systems. The cue is the scale word: 'one star' means solar system, 'billions of stars' means galaxy, and a group of galaxies is a galaxy cluster.

questions.stem: What is a black hole's event horizon?
options: The boundary from inside which not even light can escape
The dense point at the centre where almost all the mass sits
The disc of superheated gas spiralling in and giving off X-rays
The outer limit of where its gravity can affect other objects
questions.explanation: The event horizon is a boundary, not an object: once anything crosses it, the escape velocity exceeds the speed of light, so no signal can get back out. The option describing the dense central point is the singularity, which lies well inside the event horizon rather than being it. Remember that a black hole's gravity, like any mass's gravity, keeps acting at large distances — the horizon marks escape, not the end of gravitational influence.

questions.stem: A telescope is used to photograph a galaxy that is 50 million light-years from Earth. What is actually recorded in the image?
options: The galaxy exactly as it is at this moment, because light from galaxies arrives essentially instantly
The galaxy as it appeared 50 years ago, since a light-year is a measure of time rather than distance
The galaxy as it will appear in 50 million years, because its light travels ahead of the galaxy itself
The galaxy as it appeared 50 million years ago, when the light that arrived now first left it
questions.explanation: A light-year is the distance light covers in one year, so light from an object 50 million light-years away has been travelling for 50 million years and shows the object as it was then. The tempting choice is the one saying the image shows the galaxy as it is now — but light has a finite speed, and over cosmic distances the travel time is enormous. The cue: 'light-year' always converts directly into look-back time in years.

questions.stem: Astronomers observe stars forming inside cold clouds of gas and dust. What causes a star to begin shining in such a cloud?
options: Dust grains collide and set off chemical reactions that heat the cloud until it glows steadily
The cloud's rapid spin creates friction that melts the gas and holds the new star together
Gravity pulls the cloud material together until the core is hot and dense enough for hydrogen fusion
The cloud cools so far that the gases freeze solid and then begin burning chemically like a fuel
questions.explanation: Star formation is gravity-driven: as a dense region of the cloud collapses, the material is compressed and the core temperature and pressure rise until hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium, releasing energy. The chemical-burning option is the common misconception that stars 'burn' fuel the way a fire does — stars shine by nuclear fusion, not combustion, and there is no oxygen in space to burn anything. The cue is that only fusion can supply the enormous energy a star radiates for billions of years.

questions.stem: Measurements of ordinary matter across the universe, including in the very oldest stars, consistently give about 75% hydrogen and 25% helium by mass. Why is this treated as evidence for the big bang theory?
options: It shows every element in the universe, including carbon and iron, was produced in the big bang
The hot, dense conditions in the first few minutes predict almost exactly this hydrogen-to-helium ratio
It shows stars have been steadily manufacturing helium forever, so the universe never had a beginning
It shows lighter helium has drifted outwards faster than hydrogen as the universe expanded
questions.explanation: Big bang models calculate how nuclei formed while the young universe was hot and dense, and they predict roughly three-quarters hydrogen to one-quarter helium — a prediction made before the measurements were as precise as they now are. The 'stars have always been making helium' option is the discarded steady-state idea, and it fails because even the oldest, least processed stars already show this helium level. Heavier elements such as carbon and iron were made later inside stars, not in the big bang.

questions.stem: Current estimates place the age of the universe at about 13.8 billion years. Which line of evidence contributes most directly to that figure?
options: Counting the stars in the Milky Way and multiplying by a typical stellar lifetime of ten billion years
Dating the oldest rock layers found on Earth and on meteorites and adding a margin for error
Measuring the temperature at the centre of the Sun and calculating how long it has been fusing
Measuring the present rate of cosmic expansion from galaxy recession and extrapolating it backwards
questions.explanation: Because galaxies are receding at rates that increase with distance, astronomers can work out how long ago all that matter was together, giving an age of roughly 13.8 billion years; this is cross-checked with the cosmic microwave background and the ages of the oldest star clusters. Dating Earth rocks and meteorites is the tempting choice, but it gives the age of the solar system, about 4.6 billion years — far younger than the universe. The cue: expansion rate gives the age of the universe, radiometric rock dating gives the age of the solar system.

questions.stem: What is a light-year a measure of?
options: Brightness
Speed
Distance
Time
questions.explanation: A light-year is how far light travels in one year, so it measures distance even though the name contains a unit of time. That name is exactly why students pick time. If it helps, read it as 'a light-journey of one year'.
questions.teaching:
The name is the trap. It ends in a unit of time, so it reads like a duration — but read it as a *journey* and it makes sense: how far something gets in a year.

That something is light, which travels about 300,000 kilometres every second. Multiply that up over a year and you get a distance of roughly 9.5 trillion kilometres. Astronomers use it because kilometres become useless at these scales: the nearest star after the Sun is about 4.2 of these units away, which is a far more workable number than 40,000,000,000,000. Whenever you meet it, mentally finish the phrase as "a light-journey of one year".

questions.stem: What holds the planets in orbit around the Sun?
options: The solar wind
Gravity
Magnetism
Air pressure
questions.explanation: Gravity is the attraction between masses, and the Sun's mass is large enough to hold every planet. Magnetism is tempting because the Sun has a magnetic field, but planets are not magnets and orbit regardless.
questions.teaching:
Two things are needed for an orbit, and both matter. A planet is moving sideways at enormous speed, and something is pulling it towards the Sun. The pull bends the straight-line motion into a curve that keeps missing.

That pull is an attraction between masses — every mass attracts every other, and it grows with mass and weakens with distance. The Sun has over 99% of the Solar System's mass, so it dominates. Magnetism is the tempting alternative because the Sun does have a powerful magnetic field, but planets are not magnets, and the same effect holds moons around planets and stars around the galactic centre regardless of any magnetism.

questions.stem: What is a galaxy?
options: A group of planets orbiting one star
A cloud of gas with no stars in it
A huge system of stars, gas and dust bound by gravity
A single very large star near the end of its long life
questions.explanation: A galaxy holds billions of stars along with gas and dust, all held together by gravity. A solar system is the tempting answer, but that is one star and its planets — our galaxy contains billions of such systems.
questions.teaching:
The scales here are worth getting in order, because the words are often used interchangeably in everyday speech and they are wildly different in size.

A star is a single object. A star with the planets going round it is a solar system. The structure this question asks about is far larger again: hundreds of billions of stars, plus vast clouds of gas and dust, all held together by their combined gravity and rotating slowly around a common centre. Ours is around 100,000 light-years across. And these structures themselves cluster into groups and superclusters. So the order runs star, system, this, cluster.

questions.stem: Which galaxy is the Sun part of?
options: The Magellanic Cloud
Orion
The Milky Way
Andromeda
questions.explanation: The Sun is one of the Milky Way's several hundred billion stars. Andromeda is the tempting choice because it is the nearest large galaxy, but it is a separate one. Orion is a constellation, not a galaxy.
questions.teaching:
On a clear night away from city lights, a faint band of light runs across the sky. That band is the reason our galaxy has the name it does — the ancient Greeks thought it looked like spilt milk.

What you are actually seeing is the disc of our own galaxy viewed edge-on from inside it, which is why it appears as a band rather than a spiral. The Sun sits about two-thirds of the way out from the centre, one of several hundred billion stars. Andromeda is the tempting wrong answer because it is the nearest large galaxy and is visible to the naked eye — but it is a separate one, about 2.5 million light-years away.

questions.stem: What is a black hole?
options: A region whose gravity is so strong light cannot escape
An empty gap between the stars where nothing exists
A star that has completely stopped burning and gone cold
A hole in space that leads somewhere else
questions.explanation: A black hole is matter packed so densely that nothing, not even light, moves fast enough to leave. Calling it an empty gap is the common misreading — it is the opposite, an extreme concentration of mass.
questions.teaching:
The name misleads people into picturing an empty space or a tunnel through to somewhere else. It is the opposite of empty.

What it describes is matter compressed so densely that the gravity near it becomes overwhelming. Escaping any object needs a certain speed, and here that required speed exceeds the speed of light — so nothing at all can get out once past the boundary, light included, which is why it appears black. They form when a very massive star collapses at the end of its life. We detect them by what they do to their surroundings: stars orbiting apparently nothing, and matter heating up violently as it spirals in.

questions.stem: What is the main source of a star's energy?
options: Nuclear fusion in its core
Burning gas at its surface
Friction between layers of gas
Sunlight reflected from planets
questions.explanation: Stars fuse hydrogen into helium in the core, releasing enormous energy. 'Burning' is the tempting word because stars look like fire, but combustion needs oxygen and would consume a star in a moment.
questions.teaching:
Stars look like fire, and the word "burning" gets used for them constantly, but combustion is the wrong process entirely. Burning needs oxygen, and it would consume the Sun in a few thousand years — the Sun has been shining for about 4.6 billion.

What actually happens is a nuclear process, not a chemical one. Under the crushing pressure at the centre, hydrogen nuclei are forced together to form helium, and the product weighs very slightly less than the ingredients. That missing mass is released as energy, and even a tiny fraction converted this way is enormous. Gravity provides the pressure, which is why only objects above a certain mass ever ignite.

questions.stem: Why do stars appear to twinkle from Earth?
options: They rotate quickly, showing dark patches
Their light is bent by moving air in the atmosphere
They genuinely pulse brighter and dimmer every few seconds
They are partly hidden by clouds of dust in space
questions.explanation: Twinkling happens in our atmosphere: moving air bends starlight slightly and the star seems to shift and flicker. It is tempting to blame the star itself, but the same star seen from orbit shines steadily.
questions.teaching:
The clue is that planets do not twinkle nearly as much, and neither do stars seen from orbit. If the cause were in the star itself, both of those would look the same as anything else.

The cause is much closer to home: about a hundred kilometres of moving air between you and space. Pockets of air at different temperatures bend light by slightly different amounts, and as they shift the star's light wobbles and varies in brightness. A star is so far away it acts as a single point of light, so the whole point flickers. A planet shows a tiny disc, and the wobbles across it average out — which is a genuinely useful way to tell one from the other.

questions.stem: What is the Sun classified as?
options: A star
A planet
A galaxy
A comet
questions.explanation: The Sun is an ordinary star that happens to be close to us, which is why it looks so different from the others. Calling it a planet is the usual slip — planets orbit stars and produce no light of their own.
questions.teaching:
It looks nothing like the objects in the night sky, but that is entirely a matter of distance. The Sun is about 150 million kilometres away; the next nearest of its kind is 270,000 times further.

Move the Sun out to that distance and it would look like an unremarkable point of light. It is in fact a fairly average example — smaller and cooler than many, larger than most. The defining feature is that it generates its own light through nuclear fusion in its core. Planets do not: they only reflect. That distinction is the whole basis of the classification, and it is why Jupiter, however large, is in a different category.

questions.stem: What is the Big Bang theory about?
options: The explosion of one very large star in our galaxy
The collision of two galaxies
The formation of the Solar System
The universe expanding from a hot, dense state
questions.explanation: The theory describes the whole universe expanding from an extremely hot, dense beginning about 13.8 billion years ago. Picturing it as an explosion in space is the common error — space itself is what expands.
questions.teaching:
The name does a lot of damage. It suggests an explosion happening at some point within space, throwing matter outwards into an existing emptiness. That is not the picture.

The theory describes space itself expanding, everywhere at once, from an extremely hot and dense beginning about 13.8 billion years ago. There is no centre to point at and no outside to expand into — every galaxy sees every other receding from it, which is exactly what you would expect if the space between them is stretching. Two pieces of evidence support it strongly: light from distant galaxies is stretched towards the red, and a faint microwave glow fills the whole sky.

questions.stem: What is redshift evidence for?
options: Stars falling inwards
The Moon moving away
The universe expanding
The Sun cooling down
questions.explanation: Light from distant galaxies is stretched towards the red end, and the further away they are the more stretched it is. That pattern is the main evidence that the universe is expanding.
questions.teaching:
When something emitting waves moves away from you, the waves reach you stretched out. You hear it with a siren: the pitch drops as the ambulance passes. Light does the same, and stretched light is shifted towards the red end of the spectrum.

Astronomers measure this using the dark lines in a galaxy's spectrum, whose positions are known exactly. Almost every distant galaxy shows those lines shifted red — and Edwin Hubble found that the further away a galaxy is, the greater the shift. That relationship is the key part. It is what you would see if the space between everything were stretching, and it is the observation the Big Bang model was built to explain.

questions.stem: How long does sunlight take to reach Earth?
options: About 8 hours
About 8 days
About 8 minutes
About 8 seconds
questions.explanation: Light crosses the 150 million kilometres in roughly eight minutes, so you always see the Sun as it was eight minutes ago. Light from the next nearest star takes over four years.
questions.teaching:
Light is fast but not instant, and over astronomical distances the delay becomes significant enough to matter.

Light covers about 300,000 kilometres per second, and the Sun is roughly 150 million kilometres away. Divide one by the other and you get a figure in minutes rather than seconds or hours. The consequence is worth taking seriously: you never see the Sun as it is now, only as it was that many minutes ago. If it stopped shining you would not know for the same interval. The same delay applies everywhere — light from the next nearest star has been travelling over four years.

questions.stem: What is a nebula?
options: A small rocky planet
A ring around a planet
A cloud of gas and dust in space
A very old cooling star
questions.explanation: Nebulae are clouds of gas and dust, and many are the regions where new stars form as gravity pulls the material together.
questions.teaching:
Before telescopes could resolve them, astronomers used the word for any fuzzy patch in the sky, which is why the name simply means "cloud" in Latin.

What they turn out to be are vast regions of gas and dust, mostly hydrogen, spread thinly across many light-years. They matter because they are where stars come from: gravity slowly pulls denser parts of the cloud together, the centre heats as it compresses, and if enough mass gathers, fusion begins and a star switches on. Some are also the debris left when a star dies, which then seeds the next generation — so the cycle runs both ways.

questions.stem: What eventually happens to a star like the Sun?
options: It explodes as a supernova immediately
It cools slowly without changing size
It becomes a red giant, then a white dwarf
It collapses directly into a black hole instead
questions.explanation: A star of the Sun's mass swells into a red giant, sheds its outer layers and leaves a white dwarf. Supernovae and black holes need far more massive stars, which is what makes them tempting but wrong here.
questions.teaching:
A star's whole life story is decided by one thing: its mass. Stars of very different masses end very differently, so the question is really asking which path an average-mass star takes.

For the Sun, hydrogen in the core will eventually run low. The core contracts and heats while the outer layers swell enormously and cool to a red glow, engulfing the inner planets. Those outer layers then drift away, leaving the exposed hot core — small, dense and slowly cooling — behind. Supernovae, neutron stars and black holes are all real endings, but they require far greater mass, which is what makes them tempting but wrong for a star like this one.

questions.stem: Why can we see stars that may no longer exist?
options: They keep shining after they die
Our eyes retain the image
They are reflected by the Moon
Their light takes years to reach us
questions.explanation: Light travels fast but the distances are enormous, so you see a star as it was when the light left it. For distant stars that can be thousands of years ago.
questions.teaching:
This follows directly from the fact that light takes time to travel. Nothing exotic is going on — the distances are simply enormous.

Light from a star 2,000 light-years away set out 2,000 years ago, and that is the only information about it you can possibly have. Whatever it did since is still on its way. So every view of the night sky is a view of many different moments at once, each object shown as it was when its light departed. If a distant star exploded last century, the sky would look unchanged for as long as it takes that news to arrive. Nothing about human eyesight is involved.
